docs.title: Keepsake Backup
docs.text:
Keepsake Backup backs up folders of Windows servers and PCs into encrypted, compressed and deduplicated repositories – on a local disk, a network share, rotating USB disks or an SFTP server – and restores them, also on another computer without the original server, its configuration or its Windows domain.

It runs on Windows Server 2008 R2 SP1 and Windows 10/11 (x64). A Windows service runs the backups on their schedules; the Keepsake Backup program and the keepsake command line manage it.

Help for the page you are on

Press F1 in Keepsake Backup to open the help page of the current page, job editor tab or dialog. Help in the sidebar opens this overview.

docs.title: How Keepsake works
docs.text:
• Repository. Each backup job writes into its own repository: a folder (or SFTP path) with encrypted pack files. Files are split into chunks; a chunk that is already stored – from an earlier backup or another file – is not stored again. That makes every backup small after the first one.
  • Snapshots. Every backup run creates a snapshot: a complete point-in-time image you can restore on its own. Incremental and full only describe how changes are found, not what a restore needs.
  • Encryption. Everything in the repository – contents, file names, folder structure – is encrypted with AES-256-GCM. The storage operator only sees opaque files. The repository password or the recovery key opens it.
  • Self-describing. The location plus the password or recovery key are all a restore needs. No database, no configuration of the old server.
  • Service. The Keepsake Backup Service runs as LocalSystem, independent of a logged-on user. Closing the program never stops a backup.

docs.title: Keepsake Backup – Disaster Recovery Runbook
docs.text: This runbook is for the day something is gone. Print it and keep it with the KeePass export of the recovery keys. Every scenario works on any Windows computer with the .NET Framework 4.8 – the original server, its configuration and its Windows domain are not needed.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Item Where it is The backup repository the folder / network share / USB disk / SFTP server of the job The repository password or the recovery key (KS1-…) – either one is enough. A saved key file contains the same KS1-… text. The application password is not needed KeePass For SFTP: the location sftp://user@host:port/path exactly as in the job, password or private key, host key fingerprint. The account needs write access: a restore writes a temporary lock file into the repository KeePass keepsake.exe preferred: the portable ZIP or the MSI from the official release (keep a copy and its SHA-256 from SHA256SUMS.txt with the KeePass entry). Fallback: tools\keepsake-<version>\ inside every repository – see the warning below

Test this runbook once on a second computer before you rely on Keepsake (see the end of this document). Which password or key is which: PASSWORDS-AND-KEYS.md.

docs.title: Scenario 1 – The server is gone, the backups are on a share, USB disk or folder
docs.text:
1. On any Windows computer, make the repository reachable (plug in the USB disk, open the share).
  2. Unpack the portable ZIP (or install the MSI) on the local disk, e.g. C:\Keepsake, and open a command prompt there.

Copy in the repository: tools\keepsake-<version> works too, but it is not encrypted – whoever controls the backup storage could have replaced it. Before you type a password into it, check it: Get-AuthenticodeSignature .\keepsake.exe must show a valid signature of Kraus-Ahma IT Consulting (signed releases), or Get-FileHash of the files must match the release you recorded. The service re-checks this copy after every backup and repairs it, but on disaster day that service is gone. 3. With the GUI (easiest): start recovery mode and confirm the administrator prompt – - installed with the MSI: Start menu → Keepsake Recovery, or in Keepsake Backup the link Restore from a backup location… on the first-start, login and Restore pages; - portable ZIP: double-click Keepsake Recovery.cmd (or run KeepsakeGui.exe --recovery).

Enter the repository location (e.g. E:\Keepsake\Fileserver) and the password or the recovery key, click Open backup, pick the point in time, tick what you need, choose a target folder and Start restore. Show log lists anything that could not be restored. No application password, no job and no configuration are needed; the old server's settings play no role. Restore into a new folder unless the original drives and folders exist on this computer.

If the lost computer crashed during a cleanup less than 30 minutes ago, its lock still blocks the backup. Keepsake then shows whose lock it is and offers to remove it – do so when that computer is the lost one.

With the command line – list the backups:

keepsake snapshots --repo E:\Keepsake\Fileserver

Enter the repository password when asked. With the recovery key instead:

keepsake snapshots --repo E:\Keepsake\Fileserver --use-recovery-key
  1. Restore everything from the newest backup into a new folder:
keepsake restore latest --repo E:\Keepsake\Fileserver --target D:\Restore --log D:\Restore\restore.log

The files end up under D:\Restore\<drive>\<original path>. They get the permissions of D:\Restore – NTFS permissions are not part of the backup, so the files are always readable.

  1. Check restore.log for files that could not be restored.

docs.title: Scenario 2 – The backups are on an SFTP server
docs.text:
Same as scenario 1, with the SFTP location (the tools folder can be downloaded with any SFTP client, e.g. WinSCP):

keepsake snapshots --repo sftp://backup@nas.example.org/backups/fileserver

Keepsake shows the server's host key fingerprint and asks whether to trust it. Compare it with the fingerprint stored in KeePass. For scripts, pass it directly and use files for the secrets:

keepsake restore latest --repo sftp://backup@nas.example.org/backups/fileserver --sftp-host-key SHA256:... --sftp-password-file sftp.txt --recovery-key-file key.txt --target D:\Restore

With a private key: --sftp-key-file id_ed25519 (and --sftp-key-passphrase-file).

docs.title: Scenario 3 – Only some files or folders are needed
docs.text:
Browse the snapshot, then restore just that part:

keepsake ls latest --repo E:\Keepsake\Fileserver D:\Data\Finance

keepsake restore latest --repo E:\Keepsake\Fileserver --include D:\Data\Finance\2026 --target D:\Restore --flat

--flat puts 2026 directly into D:\Restore instead of recreating the full path. To restore an older state, use a snapshot ID from keepsake snapshots instead of latest.

If the Keepsake service still runs on the server, the GUI (Restore page) does the same with a folder tree.

docs.title: Scenario 4 – Restore into the original location on a rebuilt server
docs.text:
keepsake restore latest --repo E:\Keepsake\Fileserver --original --conflict newer

--conflict decides what happens with existing files: skip (default), newer, overwrite, rename. Run with --dry-run first to see what would happen.

docs.title: Scenario 5 – The password is lost
docs.text:
Use the recovery key from KeePass (--use-recovery-key or --recovery-key-file). Then set a new password so the service can continue:

keepsake key add-password --repo E:\Keepsake\Fileserver --use-recovery-key

Update the job in the GUI with the new password. Remove the old password key with keepsake key list / keepsake key remove <id> if it may have leaked.

If both the password and the recovery key are lost, the backups cannot be decrypted – by design.

docs.title: Scenario 6 – The repository reports errors
docs.text:
1. Find out what is wrong:
keepsake check --repo E:\Keepsake\Fileserver --read-data --log check.log
  1. If index files are missing or damaged ("index file cannot be read", "pack is not referenced"):
keepsake repair --repo E:\Keepsake\Fileserver

  1. Check again. Remaining errors name the affected files ("data block … is missing – the file cannot be restored"). Everything else is still restorable; restore it now, then investigate the storage (disk errors, interrupted copies).

  2. If the repository is locked by a crashed process ("in use by … since …"):

keepsake unlock --repo E:\Keepsake\Fileserver

docs.title: Scenario 7 – Set up Keepsake again on a new server
docs.text:
1. Install Keepsake (MSI), open the GUI, set the application password.
  2. Create a job with the same destination and the repository password. Keepsake recognises the existing repository ("Repository found, password correct – N snapshots") and continues it; the first backup reads all files again but only stores what changed.

docs.title: Recovery test (do this before going live, then once a year)
docs.text:
Quick check in between (or right after creating a job): Backup jobs → Check keys tests the password and the recovery key from KeePass against the job's repository without restoring anything; on the command line keepsake key verify --repo <location> --recovery-key-file key.txt (exit code 0 = valid, 4 = not valid). It does not replace the test below, which also proves the restore works without the server.

  • [ ] On a computer that is not the backup server, with only the KeePass entry at hand:
  • [ ] Unpack the portable ZIP from the KeePass attachment / release (not the copy in the repository), check its SHA-256.
  • [ ] Keepsake Recovery.cmd (portable) or Start menu → Keepsake Recovery (MSI) → open the backup with the recovery key (not the password) – the backups are listed.
  • [ ] keepsake snapshots with the recovery key – same list on the command line.
  • [ ] Restore one folder with --include … --flat into a temp folder; open some files.
  • [ ] keepsake check --read-data-percent 10 – no errors.
  • [ ] Note the date and result in the IT documentation.

docs.title: Keepsake Backup Repository Format – Version 1
docs.text: This document describes how Keepsake stores backups, precisely enough to write an independent reader (requirement REP-10). Everything uses standard, published algorithms.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
A repository is a folder (local disk, USB disk, network share; later SFTP) with this layout:

keepsake.json          plain text   header: format, version, repository ID
README.txt             plain text   how to restore, for humans
config                 encrypted    chunking and pack parameters
keys/<id>              plain text   key slots: the master key, wrapped by a password or recovery key
data/<xx>/<pack-id>    encrypted    pack files with the actual file contents and folder listings
index/<id>             encrypted    which blob is stored in which pack, at which offset
snapshots/<id>         encrypted    one file per backup run
locks/<id>             encrypted    in-use markers
tools/keepsake-<ver>/  plain        portable keepsake.exe with its libraries (for restores without installation)

<xx> is the first two hex characters of the pack ID. Content-addressed IDs (packs, blobs, index files, snapshots) are 64 lowercase hex characters; random IDs (repository, key slots, locks) are 32. Readers ignore files whose name does not match (they are never parsed or deleted). All IDs are lowercase hex (256 bits). Files whose name contains .tmp- are incomplete uploads and must be ignored.

The repository is self-describing: storage location + password (or recovery key) are enough to restore. No local database or configuration is needed.

docs.title: 2. Algorithms
docs.text: Purpose Algorithm Encryption AES-256-GCM, random 96-bit nonce, 128-bit tag Password → key Argon2id (version 0x13), parameters stored per key slot Key derivation HKDF-SHA256 (RFC 5869) Blob IDs HMAC-SHA256 with a repository-specific key File IDs (packs, index, snapshots) SHA-256 of the stored (encrypted) bytes Chunking FastCDC with normalized chunking, keyed gear table Compression Zstandard (RFC 8878), level 3 Serialization UTF-8 JSON, camelCase property names

docs.title: 2.1 Sealed data
docs.text: Seal(key, plaintext, ad) produces nonce (12 bytes) || ciphertext || tag (16 bytes) using AES-256-GCM with associated data ad. Where associated data is used, it is the UTF-8 string keepsake/v1/<kind>, binding the ciphertext to its purpose (a snapshot cannot be swapped for an index).

docs.title: 2.2 Codec envelope
docs.text:
Every encrypted payload is prefixed with one codec byte before encryption:

Byte Meaning 0x00 Stored: the rest is the raw data 0x01 Zstandard: the rest is one Zstandard frame (with content size)

Compression is only used when it saves at least ~3 %; known compressed formats (zip, jpg, mp4, docx, …) are never compressed.

docs.title: 3.1 Master key and derived keys
docs.text:
The repository has one random 32-byte master key. It never changes. With salt = repository ID bytes (hex-decoded id from keepsake.json):

encryptionKey = HKDF(master, salt, "keepsake/v1/encryption", 32)
idKey         = HKDF(master, salt, "keepsake/v1/blob-id",    32)
chunkerKey    = HKDF(master, salt, "keepsake/v1/chunker",    32)

docs.title: 3.2 Key slots (keys/<random id>)
docs.text:
Plain JSON. The master key is wrapped by a key-encryption key (KEK):

{
  "version": 1,
  "type": "password",
  "label": "Initial password",
  "created": "2026-10-17T11:43:17Z",
  "host": "FILESERVER",
  "kdf": { "algorithm": "argon2id", "version": 19, "memoryKiB": 65536, "iterations": 3, "parallelism": 2, "salt": "<base64>" },
  "data": "<base64 Seal(KEK, payload, 'keepsake/v1/key/<repository id>')>"
}
  • password slots: KEK = Argon2id(UTF-8(NFC(password)), kdf) (32 bytes).
  • recovery slots have "salt": "<base64 16 bytes>" instead of kdf: KEK = HKDF(recoveryKey, salt, "keepsake/v1/recovery-kek", 32).
  • payload is the JSON {"masterKey":"<base64>"}.

To open a repository, try every slot of the matching type; the slot whose GCM tag verifies holds the master key. Adding or removing passwords never re-encrypts data.

docs.title: 3.3 Recovery key text form
docs.text: KS1- followed by Crockford Base32 (0123456789ABCDEFGHJKMNPQRSTVWXYZ, most significant bit first) of recoveryKey (32 bytes) || first 2 bytes of SHA-256(recoveryKey), in groups of five separated by -. When reading, case, spaces and dashes are ignored, O reads as 0, I/L as 1.

docs.title: 4. Encrypted files
docs.text:
config, index/*, snapshots/* and locks/* have the layout

0x01 || Seal(encryptionKey, codec || JSON, "keepsake/v1/<kind>")

with kind config, index, snapshot or lock. For index/* and snapshots/* the file name is the SHA-256 of the complete file, so damage is detectable without the key.

docs.title: 4.1 config
docs.text: { "chunkerMin": 524288, "chunkerAvg": 1048576, "chunkerMax": 8388608, "packSize": 16777216, "compression": "zstd" }

docs.title: 5. Blobs and packs
docs.text:
A blob is either a chunk of file content (data) or a folder listing (tree).

  • Blob ID = HMAC-SHA256(idKey, plaintext). Identical content always has the same ID, which is how deduplication works. Keying the HMAC prevents outsiders from confirming that a known file is stored.
  • Stored blob = Seal(encryptionKey, codec || plaintext, no associated data).

A pack file concatenates stored blobs and ends with a header:

blob_1 || blob_2 || … || blob_n || Seal(encryptionKey, header, "keepsake/v1/pack-header") || uint32 LE length of the sealed header

Plain header:

0x01 (version) || uint32 LE n || n × entry
entry = type (1 byte: 0 data, 1 tree) || blob ID (32 bytes) || uint32 LE stored length || uint32 LE plaintext length

Blob offsets follow from the order and lengths (first blob at offset 0). Data blobs and tree blobs are kept in separate packs. Pack ID = SHA-256 of the complete pack file. Packs are about 16 MiB.

docs.title: 5.1 Chunking
docs.text:
FastCDC over the file content with min/avg/max from config:

  • gear[i] = first 8 bytes (little-endian uint64) of HMAC-SHA256(chunkerKey, uint32 LE i) for i = 0…255.
  • bits = floor(log2(avg)), maskS = top bits+2 bits set, maskL = top bits-2 bits set.
  • Starting at offset min with fp = 0: fp = (fp << 1) + gear[byte]; cut after the byte where fp & maskS == 0 (before avg) or fp & maskL == 0 (between avg and max); cut at max at the latest.
  • Files smaller than min are one chunk. Empty files have no chunks.

Readers do not need the chunker: a file's content is simply its blobs concatenated in order.

docs.title: 6. Index (index/<id>)
docs.text:
{ "packs": [ { "id": "<pack id>", "blobs": [ { "id": "<blob id>", "type": "data", "offset": 0, "length": 1048604, "rawLength": 1048576 } ] } ] }

The union of all index files maps blob ID → pack, offset, stored length. A pack appears in an index only after it has been completely written. If an index is lost, it can be rebuilt from the pack headers.

docs.title: 7. Trees
docs.text:
A tree blob is the JSON of one folder listing, nodes sorted by name (ordinal):

{ "nodes": [
  { "name": "report.xlsx", "type": "file", "size": 48213, "mTime": 638640000000000000, "cTime": 638640000000000000, "attributes": 32, "content": ["<blob id>", "…"] },
  { "name": "2026", "type": "dir", "size": 0, "mTime": 638640000000000000, "cTime": 638640000000000000, "attributes": 0, "subtree": "<tree blob id>" }
] }
  • Times are UTC .NET ticks (100 ns intervals since 0001-01-01 00:00 UTC).
  • attributes: Windows file attributes, limited to read-only (1), hidden (2), system (4), archive (32) and not-content-indexed (8192).
  • NTFS permissions are not stored.

docs.title: 7.1 Path mapping
docs.text:
The root tree of a snapshot represents the whole machine:

Windows path Path in the snapshot D:\Data\Finance D/Data/Finance \\server\share\Projects UNC/server/share/Projects

Folders above the selected sources (D, D/Data) are included only as far as needed to reach them.

docs.title: 8. Snapshots (snapshots/<id>)
docs.text:
{
  "version": 1,
  "time": "2026-10-17T11:43:17Z",
  "host": "FILESERVER", "user": "DOMAIN\\SYSTEM", "job": "fileserver",
  "paths": ["D:\\Data"], "excludes": ["*.tmp"], "tags": [],
  "mode": "incremental",
  "tree": "<root tree blob id>",
  "parent": "<previous snapshot id>",
  "program": "Keepsake 0.1.0",
  "summary": { "filesNew": 12, "filesChanged": 3, "filesUnchanged": 49985, "filesSkipped": 0, "dirs": 6500,
               "totalBytes": 139586437120, "bytesRead": 1288490188, "bytesAdded": 356515840, "bytesStored": 125829120, "durationSeconds": 92.4 }
}

Every snapshot is complete on its own: incremental and full only describe how changes were detected (full re-reads every file), not what is needed for a restore.

docs.title: 9. Locks (locks/<random id>)
docs.text:
{ "host": "FILESERVER", "user": "…", "pid": 4242, "time": "…", "exclusive": false, "purpose": "backup" }

Backup, restore and check take shared locks; operations that delete data take an exclusive lock. Locks are refreshed every 5 minutes and count as stale after 30 minutes.

docs.title: 10. Write order and crash safety
docs.text:
1. Pack files are written (temp file + rename).
  2. Index files listing those packs are written every 20 packs / 5 minutes and at the end.
  3. The snapshot is written last.

A crash or cancellation can leave packs without an index (reported by check, removed by a later prune) or an index without a snapshot (reused by the next backup) – never a snapshot that points to missing data.

docs.title: 11. Restoring without Keepsake (outline)
docs.text:
1. Read keepsake.json; derive the KEK from the password with the slot's Argon2id parameters; open the slot; derive encryptionKey.
  2. Decrypt all index/* files to map blob IDs to packs.
  3. Decrypt the wanted snapshots/* file, then walk the trees from tree.
  4. For each file, read its blobs from the packs (offset/length from the index), open each with AES-256-GCM, strip the codec byte (decompress if 0x01), and concatenate.

docs.title: Keepsake Backup – Passwords and keys
docs.text: Keepsake uses one application password per computer and, per backup repository, a password and a recovery key. They protect different things. This page says which one you need when.

docs.title: The short version
docs.text:
To restore on any Windows computer you need:

  1. access to the repository (folder, network share, USB disk, or for SFTP: server, user and password/private key), and
  2. either the repository password or the recovery key (KS1-…) – one of the two is enough.

If both the repository password and the recovery key are lost, the backups cannot be decrypted by anyone. Keep both in KeePass, and keep a copy of the KeePass database off the server that is backed up.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Application password Repository password Recovery key (KS1-…) Destination credentials Protects Access to the Keepsake service on this computer (GUI and CLI) The backups of one repository (encryption) The backups of one repository (encryption) Access to the storage: share, SFTP server Set First start of the GUI, or keepsake setup When the repository is created (job editor, or keepsake init) Generated automatically when the repository is created; shown once In the job editor (share credentials, SFTP login, host key) How many One per computer One per repository; more can be added One per repository; more can be added Per job Stored on the server Only as a hash (config\settings.json) Encrypted for the service (config\jobs.json), so scheduled backups run unattended Never – only you have it Encrypted for the service (config\jobs.json) Needed to restore on another computer No Yes – this or the recovery key Yes – this or the password Yes If lost Not critical: the backups are unaffected; an administrator can reset the service configuration Use the recovery key and add a new password Create a new one with the password (keepsake key add-recovery) Ask the storage administrator / provider

docs.title: Application password
docs.text: Only guards the Keepsake service on this computer against casual use. It cannot decrypt anything, and it is useless on another computer. Local administrators can get around it (they can edit the configuration). Change it under Settings → Application password; that does not affect any repository.

docs.title: Repository password
docs.text: Encrypts the backups of a repository. Keepsake stores a copy on the server (protected with Windows DPAPI for the service account), which is why scheduled backups and restores on the Restore page never ask for it. That copy only works on this server – on another computer you type the password (or the recovery key) yourself.

docs.title: Recovery key
docs.text:
A second, independent way into the same repository. It is 256 bits of random data, so it cannot be guessed, and it keeps working when passwords are added, changed or removed. Use it when the password is forgotten or was stored wrongly. Keepsake does not keep a copy: if it was not stored when it was shown, create a new one with keepsake key add-recovery (which needs the password).

"Key file": there is no separate key file. Save as file… (GUI) or --recovery-key-out (CLI) writes the same KS1-… text into a text file (keepsake-recovery-key.txt, readable only by you). Load from file… and --recovery-key-file read it back; pasting the text works just as well. Case, spaces and dashes do not matter.

The password and the recovery key are equally powerful: whoever has either one plus access to the repository can read all backups.

docs.title: Where to keep what (KeePass)
docs.text:
Keepsake prepares the entry: when a repository is created, Copy KeePass entry in the recovery key dialog copies a text block with the location, host key, login hints and the recovery key (Save as file… saves the same block; it also works as a recovery key file). For an existing job, Copy for KeePass on the job editor's Destination tab copies the same block without the recovery key. Passwords are never part of it: add them yourself.

One entry per backup job:

  • repository location (folder, share, USB disk label, or sftp://user@host:port/path)
  • repository password
  • recovery key (KS1-…) – as text or the saved key file as attachment
  • for SFTP: user, password or private key (+ passphrase), host key fingerprint (SHA256:…). The account needs write access even for a restore: Keepsake writes a temporary lock file into the repository
  • for shares: user and password, if the job uses its own share credentials

Plus, once: the application password of each server, and the portable ZIP of the installed version with its SHA-256 from SHA256SUMS.txt.

docs.title: Checking that the stored keys work
docs.text:
Test the password and the recovery key from KeePass right after creating a job and from time to time:

  • GUI: Backup jobs → Check keys on the job – only the repository's key files are read, nothing is restored or changed.
  • Command line (also without the service): keepsake key verify --repo <location> --recovery-key-file key.txt or --password-file pw.txt; exit code 0 = valid, 4 = not valid.

Once a year, do the full recovery test from DISASTER-RECOVERY.md on a second computer.

docs.title: Managing keys
docs.text:
All on the command line, with the current password or recovery key (keepsake help key):

Task Command List the keys of a repository keepsake key list --repo <location> Add a password (e.g. the old one is forgotten) keepsake key add-password --repo <location> --use-recovery-key Create an additional recovery key keepsake key add-recovery --repo <location> --recovery-key-out key.txt Remove a key keepsake key remove <id> --repo <location> (the last key cannot be removed)

After adding a new repository password, enter it in the job editor as well, so the service uses it.

Removing a key does not revoke it for someone who kept a copy of the repository's key files and knows that password or key. After a leak, create a new repository and let the old one expire.

docs.title: Keepsake Backup on Windows Server 2008 R2
docs.text: Keepsake targets Windows Server 2008 R2 SP1 and Windows 10/11. Everything it uses exists on 2008 R2, but a few prerequisites are not there by default. keepsake doctor checks all of them.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Item Why How Service Pack 1 (build 7601) .NET Framework 4.8 requires it Windows Update / KB976932 .NET Framework 4.8 runtime of all Keepsake programs offline installer ndp48-x86-x64-allos-enu.exe (KB4503548) 64-bit Windows the MSI is x64 2008 R2 is 64-bit only TLS 1.2 for clients e-mail notifications (STARTTLS/SSL); not needed for SFTP or file shares Enable-Tls12.ps1 in the install folder (elevated) + reboot Volume Shadow Copy service not disabled backing up open files services.msc → Volume Shadow Copy → Manual Up-to-date root certificates SMTP servers with public certificates root certificate update / Windows Update

Notes:

  • 2008 R2 is out of support. Keep the server off the internet as far as possible and store the backups off this server (share, USB rotation, SFTP).
  • The GUI needs the "Desktop Experience"-free WPF of .NET 4.8 – nothing else to install.
  • Paths longer than 260 characters work (Keepsake uses \\?\ paths internally).
  • Internet Explorer is not used.
  • SFTP and AES-CTR. On 2008 R2 with .NET Framework 4.8, SSH.NET's AES-CTR (Windows AES provider) failed with "MAC error" – e.g. a Hetzner Storage Box on port 22 (ProFTPD mod_sftp, AES-CTR only), which works from Windows 10/11. AES-GCM (no HMAC) worked. Since 0.9.8 Keepsake computes AES-CTR and all HMACs with BouncyCastle (ManagedAesCtrCipher, ManagedHmac), like AES-GCM and ChaCha20, and prefers AEAD ciphers anyway. keepsake sftp-test --repo sftp://… shows which algorithms work from this computer. (Hetzner Storage Box: port 23 is OpenSSH with AES-GCM, port 22 is mod_sftp; the job editor offers "Use port 23", which confirms port 23's own host key and checks that the repository is found there.) For support, switch on Settings → Write a debug log (%ProgramData%\Keepsake\logs\debug.log), or in the portable recovery mode the checkbox under Open backup (%TEMP%\keepsake-debug.log).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
1. Install the prerequisites, reboot.
  2. Run Keepsake-<version>.msi (as administrator). It installs to C:\Program Files\dkait\keepsake (or a folder you choose in the setup), registers and starts the Keepsake Backup Service (LocalSystem, automatic, restarts on failure), adds keepsake to the PATH and creates the Start menu entries Keepsake Backup and Keepsake Recovery.
  3. Open Keepsake Backup, set the application password, create the first job.
  4. Run keepsake doctor in an elevated prompt – everything should be OK or INFO.

Configuration and history live in %ProgramData%\Keepsake and survive upgrades and uninstalls.

docs.title: Test plan (run on a 2008 R2 SP1 VM before production)
docs.text:
Tick each item; note deviations.

Installation - [ ] MSI refuses to install without .NET 4.8 (clear message). - [ ] MSI installs; service is running and set to automatic; keepsake works in a new prompt. - [ ] keepsake doctor (elevated) shows no FAIL; WARN only for TLS 1.2 before running the script. - [ ] Enable-Tls12.ps1 (install folder) + reboot → doctor shows TLS 1.2 OK.

GUI - [ ] Start menu entry starts the GUI with a UAC prompt; first-time setup and login work. - [ ] Start menu entry Keepsake Recovery (and the link on the first-start screen) opens recovery mode without a login. - [ ] Folder tree shows all drives; tick/untick works; long folder names display. - [ ] Job with a folder destination: repository created, recovery key dialog requires confirmation. - [ ] Job with a USB disk: disk listed with label; after re-plugging under another letter the backup still finds it. - [ ] Job with a network share and its own credentials: check destination OK; backup works while the service account has no access to the share. - [ ] Job with SFTP: host key prompt; backup works.

Backup - [ ] Open Outlook PST / locked Office file is backed up (VSS); log shows no "locked" errors. - [ ] Folder whose ACL excludes Administrators is backed up (backup privilege). - [ ] Path longer than 260 characters is backed up and restored. - [ ] Incremental run after no changes takes seconds for the real data set (~50,000 files). - [ ] Initial ~200 GB backup completes; cancel in the middle → next run continues without re-uploading. - [ ] Scheduled run at the configured time; machine off at that time → catch-up after start.

Maintenance and alerts - [ ] Cleanup after a backup removes snapshots according to the rules; protected snapshot survives. - [ ] Scheduled check runs; --read-data check reports 0 errors. - [ ] Test e-mail arrives; a failed run sends a mail; "no successful backup" alert after the set hours. - [ ] Event Log: entries 1000/1001/1002 appear under source Keepsake.

Restore and disaster recovery - [ ] Restore single files to another folder and to the original location (each conflict policy once). - [ ] Follow DISASTER-RECOVERY.md scenario 1 on a second computer using only the recovery key. - [ ] Uninstall: service removed, %ProgramData%\Keepsake kept; reinstall picks the jobs up again.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text: keepsake.exe is the command-line interface of Keepsake Backup. It does two jobs. It works directly on a repository without the service: create one, back up, list, restore, check, clean up and manage keys. It also controls the running Keepsake service: import and export jobs, start and cancel runs, read the run history and logs. Every command can print machine-readable JSON and returns a defined exit code, so you can drive Keepsake from scripts, scheduled tasks and monitoring systems.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Where it is. The MSI installs keepsake.exe into the program folder (by default C:\Program Files\dkait\keepsake) and adds that folder to the PATH, so keepsake works in any new command prompt. The portable ZIP (Keepsake-<version>-portable.zip) contains the same keepsake.exe. Extract it and run it from that folder. The repository commands need nothing else than .NET Framework 4.8, which makes the portable ZIP useful for restoring on a replacement computer (see Disaster recovery).

Elevation. The service accepts connections from elevated administrators only, so run the service commands from an elevated prompt ("Run as administrator"). The repository commands do not need elevation as such. Your account still has to be able to read the files you back up, write to the repository and write to the restore target. Restoring to the original location under C:\ or into other protected folders usually needs an elevated prompt.

Two kinds of commands, two kinds of passwords.

Kind Commands Talks to Needs Repository commands init, backup, snapshots, ls, restore, check, prune, protect, repair, key, unlock, sftp-test The repository directly (folder, share, USB disk, SFTP). The service is not involved The repository password or a recovery key (KS1-...). Either one opens the repository on any computer. sftp-test needs only the SFTP login Service commands setup, status, jobs, run, cancel, runs, log The local Keepsake service through its named pipe The application password. It protects the service and cannot decrypt backups Tools doctor, version, help Neither (doctor only tests whether the service is reachable) Nothing

The application password and the repository passwords are separate. Mixing them up is the most common cause of exit code 4. See Passwords and keys.

Syntax. keepsake <command> [arguments] [options]. Options start with -- and may also be written as --name=value. Options and positional arguments can come in any order. Everything after a bare -- counts as a positional argument. keepsake help <command> and keepsake <command> --help show the built-in help for a command.

keepsake help restore

docs.title: Common options
docs.text:
These options are accepted by every command. A command uses only the ones that apply to it. For example, --repo matters only to repository commands.

Option Environment variable Meaning --repo <location> KEEPSAKE_REPOSITORY Repository location: a local folder (E:\Backups\fileserver), a USB disk folder, a network share (\\nas\backup\fileserver) or sftp://user@host[:port]/path (port 22 if omitted, for example sftp://backup@nas.example.org/backups/fileserver). --password-file <file> KEEPSAKE_PASSWORD Repository password, read from the first line of the file. The environment variable holds the password itself. --recovery-key-file <file> KEEPSAKE_RECOVERY_KEY Unlock with a recovery key instead of the password. The file holds the KS1-... text (a file written by --recovery-key-out works as is). The environment variable holds the key text itself. --use-recovery-key When prompting, ask for the recovery key instead of the password. --sftp-password-file <file> KEEPSAKE_SFTP_PASSWORD SFTP password (first line of the file). Without it and without a key, you are prompted. --sftp-key-file <file> SFTP private key file. When given, the SFTP password is not used. --sftp-key-passphrase-file <file> KEEPSAKE_SFTP_KEY_PASSPHRASE Passphrase of the SFTP private key (first line of the file). --sftp-host-key <SHA256:...> KEEPSAKE_SFTP_HOST_KEY Trusted host key fingerprint of the SFTP server. Without it you are asked to trust the key on first connection. --json Machine-readable JSON on stdout instead of text. Implies --quiet. Errors are printed as JSON too. --non-interactive Never prompt. A missing password fails with exit code 3. This is automatic when input is redirected or no interactive user is present (scheduled task, service). --quiet No progress line. Results are still printed. --log <file> Write a detailed run log (summary, phases, every problem) to the file. Used by backup, restore, check, prune and repair. The folder is created if needed. --debug-log <file> Write SFTP connection details (algorithms, errors, no passwords) to the file for support. --app-password-file <file> KEEPSAKE_APP_PASSWORD Application password for the service commands (first line of the file). --help Show the help of the command instead of running it.

Which credential wins. For repository commands Keepsake uses the first credential it finds, in this order:

  1. --recovery-key-file
  2. KEEPSAKE_RECOVERY_KEY
  3. --password-file
  4. KEEPSAKE_PASSWORD
  5. A prompt for the password, or for the recovery key with --use-recovery-key (not with --non-interactive)

Warning

A KEEPSAKE_RECOVERY_KEY variable that is set in the environment beats --password-file on the command line. Clear environment variables you no longer need, or a wrong credential gets used and the command fails with exit code 4.

Password files are read as text. Only the first line counts, a trailing line break is ignored and a UTF-8 byte order mark is removed. Protect these files with NTFS permissions so only the account that runs the script can read them.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 Success 1 Finished with warnings (for example some files could not be read, or doctor found warnings) 2 Failed 3 Usage error: unknown command or option, missing argument, missing password in non-interactive mode, invalid value, or a job or run the service did not accept or find 4 Wrong password, recovery key or application password (also when the service has locked out logins after failed attempts) 5 Repository locked by another process, or the service reports a conflict (for example the job is already running) 6 Cancelled (Ctrl+C, or the run was cancelled)

Press Ctrl+C once to cancel cleanly: Keepsake finishes the current block and stops (exit code 6). Press it a second time to abort immediately.

docs.title: setup
docs.text:
Sets the application password of the service. This works only once, on a service that has no application password yet. After that, change the password in the GUI under Settings.

keepsake setup [--new-password-file <file>]
Option Meaning --new-password-file <file> Read the new application password from the first line of the file. Without it you are prompted twice. Interactive entries need at least 8 characters. 
keepsake setup

keepsake setup --new-password-file C:\Keepsake\app-password.txt

docs.title: status
docs.text:
Shows the service version, host, data folder and number of parallel jobs, followed by one line per job: state (idle, running, waiting, disabled), last run, result and next run. For running jobs it adds a progress line.

keepsake status [--app-password-file <file>]

No options of its own besides --app-password-file and the common options.

keepsake status

keepsake status --json --app-password-file C:\Keepsake\app-password.txt

docs.title: jobs
docs.text:
Lists, shows, exports, imports and removes the backup jobs of the service. <job> is the job name (not case-sensitive) or its full ID.

keepsake jobs [list]
keepsake jobs show <job>
keepsake jobs export <job> [--out <file>]
keepsake jobs import <file> [--repository-password-file <file>]
keepsake jobs remove <job>
Subcommand What it does list (default) One line per job: short ID, name, enabled/disabled, destination, and the schedules (or manual only). show <job> Details of one job: destination, sources, exclusions, schedules, next run, missed-run handling, retries and pre/post commands. Shows (NO PASSWORD STORED) if the service has no repository password for the job. export <job> Writes the job definition as JSON, without passwords. Writes to stdout, or to the file given with --out. import <file> Creates a job from a JSON file. If a job with the same ID or name already exists, it is updated instead. remove <job> Deletes the job from the service. The repository and its backups are not touched. Option Meaning --out <file> export: write the JSON to this file instead of stdout. --repository-password-file <file> import: repository password of the job's destination (first line of the file). A new job needs it: without the option you are prompted, and with --non-interactive the import fails. When an existing job is updated, the stored password is kept unless you give a new one.

The destination repository must already exist when you import a new job. Create it with keepsake init or in the GUI.

keepsake jobs

keepsake jobs export fileserver --out D:\Keepsake\fileserver-job.json

keepsake jobs import D:\Keepsake\fileserver-job.json --repository-password-file C:\Keepsake\repo-password.txt

docs.title: Job file format
docs.text:
The file is the JSON produced by jobs export. Property names use camelCase and enum values are lower-case strings. Properties you leave out get their defaults. A minimal job:

{
  "name": "fileserver",
  "sources": ["D:\\Data"],
  "excludes": ["*.tmp", "D:\\Data\\**\\cache\\"],
  "destination": { "type": "folder", "path": "\\\\nas\\backup\\fileserver" },
  "schedules": [
    { "kind": "daily", "times": ["22:00"], "mode": "incremental" },
    { "kind": "daily", "times": ["23:30"], "weekdays": ["sunday"], "mode": "full" }
  ],
  "retention": { "keepDaily": 14, "keepWeekly": 8, "keepMonthly": 12 },
  "retryCount": 2,
  "retryDelayMinutes": 15
}
Property Default Meaning name (required) Job name. Also used to match an existing job on import. enabled true Disabled jobs do not run on schedule. sources (required) Absolute paths (D:\Data, \\server\share\folder). excludes empty Exclusion patterns, see What to back up and exclusions. useDefaultExcludes true Also skip recycle bin, System Volume Information, pagefile.sys, hiberfil.sys, swapfile.sys and ~$* files. destination type: folder (absolute path), usb (path relative to the disk, for example Keepsake\\Fileserver, plus volumes) or sftp (host, port (default 22), user, auth password or key, absolute remote path, hostKeyFingerprint). See Destination. shareCredentials empty List of { "share": "\\\\server\\share", "user": "DOMAIN\\user" }. schedules empty (manual only) Entries with kind (interval, daily, monthly), intervalMinutes, times (HH:mm), weekdays (monday ... sunday, empty = every day), daysOfMonth, mode (incremental or full), enabled. See Schedule. runMissed true Run once after start-up if a scheduled run was missed. retryCount, retryDelayMinutes 2, 15 Retries after a failed run (0-10 retries, 1 minute to 24 hours apart). preCommand, postCommand, commandTimeoutMinutes none, none, 30 Commands run through cmd.exe before and after the backup. See Options. workers 0 Parallel file workers, 0 = automatic. useVss true Read from a Volume Shadow Copy so open files are backed up. retention none (keep all) keepLast, keepDaily, keepWeekly, keepMonthly, keepYearly, keepWithinDays. See Retention and checks. pruneEveryDays, checkEveryDays 7, 7 Run cleanup or a check after a backup when the last one is older (0 = never). checkReadDataPercent 10 Share of data read by scheduled checks (0 = structure only). notifyOnFailure, notifyOnWarning, notifyOnSuccess true, true, false E-mail notifications, see Monitoring and notifications. alertNoSuccessHours 0 (off) Alert when there was no successful backup for this many hours.

id, created and modified appear in an export and can stay in the file. They are managed by the service.

Note

jobs import transfers only the repository password. SFTP passwords, SFTP private keys and network share passwords cannot be set from the command line. Enter them in the job editor of the GUI after the import. Existing secrets of an updated job are kept.

docs.title: run
docs.text:
Starts a job now, the same as Run now in the GUI. By default it runs a backup. The run happens in the service, with the job's settings (VSS, retries, notifications, pre/post commands), and it appears in the run history.

keepsake run <job> [--full | --check | --full-check | --prune] [--wait]
Option Meaning --full Full backup: re-read every file instead of trusting size and modification time. --check Verify the repository instead of backing up, reading the job's sample of the data (checkReadDataPercent). --full-check Verify the repository and read all stored data. --prune Apply the job's retention rules and free unused space. --wait Show progress until the run ends, print its result and return its exit code (0, 1, 2 or 6). Ctrl+C then cancels the run in the service.

Without --wait, run returns 0 as soon as the service has accepted the run and prints the run ID. If the options are combined, --prune beats --check/--full-check, and --full only applies to backups.

keepsake run fileserver --wait

keepsake run fileserver --full --wait

keepsake run fileserver --full-check --wait --log D:\Logs\check.log

docs.title: cancel
docs.text:
Cancels a running job, or removes a job that is waiting for a free slot from the queue.

keepsake cancel <job>

keepsake cancel fileserver

docs.title: runs
docs.text:
Shows the run history, newest first: run ID, job, start, duration, result, trigger and files/data. For runs that did not succeed, the message is shown below the line.

keepsake runs [<job>] [--limit <n>]
Option Meaning <job> Only runs of this job. Default: all jobs. --limit <n> Number of runs, 1 to 1000. Default: 20. 
keepsake runs fileserver --limit 5

docs.title: log
docs.text:
Prints the full log of one run. Take the run ID from runs, from the output of run, or from History and logs in the GUI.

keepsake log <run-id>

keepsake log 20261121T210000Z-3f9a1c

docs.title: init
docs.text:
Creates a new encrypted repository with a password and a recovery key. The recovery key is shown only once. Store it in KeePass right away: without the password or the recovery key, the backups cannot be restored.

keepsake init --repo <location> [--password-file <file>] [--recovery-key-out <file>]
Option Meaning --password-file <file> Password for the new repository (or KEEPSAKE_PASSWORD). Without it you are prompted twice. Interactive entries need at least 8 characters. --recovery-key-out <file> Also write the recovery key to this file, together with location, repository ID and date. Move the file off the server afterwards.

With --json the output includes the recovery key in the recoveryKey field. Do not let a script log it in plain text.

keepsake init --repo E:\Backups\fileserver

keepsake init --repo \\nas\backup\fileserver --password-file C:\Keepsake\repo-password.txt --recovery-key-out C:\Keepsake\fileserver-recovery.txt

docs.title: backup
docs.text:
Backs up folders and files into a new snapshot. The backup is incremental: unchanged files (same size and modification time as in the previous snapshot) are not read again, and only new data is stored.

keepsake backup --repo <location> <folder-or-file>... [options]
Option Meaning <folder-or-file>... One or more folders or files to back up (required). --exclude <pattern> Exclude by name (*.tmp), folder (cache\) or path (D:\Data\**\obj\). Repeatable. See What to back up and exclusions. --exclude-file <file> Read exclusion patterns from a file: one per line, empty lines and lines starting with # are ignored. Repeatable. --no-default-excludes Also back up $RECYCLE.BIN\, System Volume Information\, pagefile.sys, hiberfil.sys, swapfile.sys and ~$* files. --full Re-read every file instead of trusting size and modification time. --job <name> Job name stored in the snapshot. Incremental backups continue from the last snapshot of this job. --tag <tag> Tag the snapshot. Repeatable. --parent <snapshot> Use this snapshot as the base for change detection instead of the latest one of the same job, host and sources. --workers <n> Files processed in parallel, 1 to 32. Default: number of processors, at most 4. --report-excluded List every excluded item in the run report and --log file.

Note

The backup command reads the live files. It does not create a Volume Shadow Copy and does not use the backup privilege the service uses. Files that are open or locked are reported as not backed up (exit code 1). For servers, configure a job and use keepsake run instead.

keepsake backup --repo E:\Backups\fileserver --job fileserver D:\Data --exclude "*.tmp" --log D:\Logs\backup.log

keepsake backup --repo E:\Backups\fileserver --job fileserver D:\Data D:\Projects --exclude-file D:\Keepsake\excludes.txt --tag before-migration

docs.title: snapshots
docs.text:
Lists the snapshots in the repository, oldest first: short ID, time, job, mode, files, size and paths. Protected snapshots are marked with *.

keepsake snapshots --repo <location> [--job <name>]
Option Meaning --job <name> Only snapshots of this job (not case-sensitive). 
keepsake snapshots --repo E:\Backups\fileserver

keepsake snapshots --repo E:\Backups\fileserver --job fileserver --json

docs.title: Selecting a snapshot
docs.text:
Wherever a command takes <snapshot>, you can give:

  • latest: the newest snapshot. Together with --job <name> (ls, restore), the newest snapshot of that job.
  • An ID or the start of an ID with at least 4 hexadecimal characters, for example 3f9a1c2e from the snapshots list. It must match exactly one snapshot.

docs.title: ls
docs.text:
Lists the contents of a snapshot: type (d folder, f file), modification time, size and path.

keepsake ls --repo <location> <snapshot|latest> [<path>] [--recursive] [--job <name>]
Option Meaning <path> Folder or file inside the snapshot, as a Windows path (D:\Data\Finance) or in snapshot form (D/Data/Finance). Default: the top level. --recursive Also list all subfolders. --job <name> With latest: the newest snapshot of this job. 
keepsake ls --repo E:\Backups\fileserver latest D:\Data\Finance

keepsake ls --repo E:\Backups\fileserver 3f9a1c2e D:\Data --recursive --json

docs.title: restore
docs.text:
Restores files from a snapshot, either into a folder or back to their original location. Without a snapshot argument, latest is used. NTFS permissions are not restored: restored files inherit the permissions of the folder they land in. More on restoring: Restoring files.

keepsake restore --repo <location> [<snapshot|latest>] (--target <folder> | --original) [options]

Give exactly one of --target or --original.

Option Meaning --target <folder> Restore into this folder. By default the full path is kept: D:\Data\Finance\x.xlsx lands in <folder>\D\Data\Finance\x.xlsx. --original Restore to the original location (D:\Data\...). --include <path> Only restore this folder or file (Windows path or snapshot path). Repeatable. Default: everything. --flat With --target: place the selected folder directly in the target (<folder>\Finance\...) instead of keeping the full path. --conflict <policy> What to do when a different file already exists: skip (default, keep the existing file), overwrite, newer (replace only if the backed-up file is newer) or rename (restore next to it as name (restored 1).ext). Files identical in size and modification time are always left alone. --no-attributes Do not restore the read-only, hidden and system attributes. --dry-run Show what would be restored without writing anything. --job <name> With latest: the newest snapshot of this job.

Files skipped because of a conflict are listed as problems and the restore finishes with warnings (exit code 1).

keepsake restore latest --repo E:\Backups\fileserver --target D:\Restore --include D:\Data\Finance --flat

keepsake restore 3f9a1c2e --repo E:\Backups\fileserver --original --include "D:\Data\Projects\Offer 2026.docx" --conflict rename

keepsake restore latest --repo sftp://backup@nas.example.org/backups/fileserver --sftp-password-file C:\Keepsake\sftp.txt --recovery-key-file C:\Keepsake\fileserver-recovery.txt --target D:\Restore --dry-run

docs.title: check
docs.text:
Verifies the repository. Without options it checks the structure: every snapshot, folder listing and data reference. With --read-data it also downloads and decrypts the stored data.

keepsake check --repo <location> [--read-data] [--read-data-percent <1-100>]
Option Meaning --read-data Read and decrypt all stored data. --read-data-percent <n> Read and decrypt a random sample of n percent of the data (1 to 100). Implies --read-data. 
keepsake check --repo E:\Backups\fileserver --read-data-percent 10

keepsake check --repo E:\Backups\fileserver --read-data --log D:\Logs\check-full.log

If check reports missing or unreadable index files, run keepsake repair.

docs.title: prune
docs.text:
Removes old snapshots by retention rules and frees the space that no snapshot uses any more. The rules combine: a snapshot is kept if any rule keeps it. Protected snapshots are always kept. Without any --keep-* option no snapshot is deleted, and only unused data is removed. See Retention and checks.

keepsake prune --repo <location> [--keep-last <n>] [--keep-daily <n>] [--keep-weekly <n>] [--keep-monthly <n>] [--keep-yearly <n>] [--keep-within <days>] [--job <name>] [--dry-run]
Option Meaning --keep-last <n> Keep the newest n snapshots. --keep-daily <n> Keep the newest snapshot of each of the last n days that have snapshots. --keep-weekly <n> The same per week. --keep-monthly <n> The same per month. --keep-yearly <n> The same per year. --keep-within <days> Keep all snapshots of the last days days. --job <name> Apply the rules only to snapshots of this job. Other snapshots stay. --dry-run Show which snapshots would be removed, without changing anything. 
keepsake prune --repo E:\Backups\fileserver --job fileserver --keep-daily 14 --keep-weekly 8 --keep-monthly 12 --dry-run

keepsake prune --repo E:\Backups\fileserver --job fileserver --keep-daily 14 --keep-weekly 8 --keep-monthly 12

docs.title: protect
docs.text:
Protects a snapshot from retention, so neither prune nor a job's cleanup ever removes it. --remove takes the protection away again. Protecting rewrites the snapshot record, so the snapshot gets a new ID, which is printed.

keepsake protect <snapshot> --repo <location> [--remove]
Option Meaning --remove Remove the protection. 
keepsake protect 3f9a1c2e --repo E:\Backups\fileserver

docs.title: repair
docs.text:
Rebuilds the repository index from the pack files. Use it when check reports missing or unreadable index files. It reads only the pack headers, writes a new index and removes the old index files. Snapshots and data are not changed. Run check afterwards to see whether any snapshot still misses data.

keepsake repair --repo <location>

keepsake repair --repo E:\Backups\fileserver --log D:\Logs\repair.log

docs.title: key
docs.text:
Manages the passwords and recovery keys of a repository. Every repository has at least one password and one recovery key (KS1-...), and each of them opens the repository on any computer. To unlock, use the repository credential options from Common options above. The application password of the service is not a repository key. Background: Passwords and keys.

keepsake key list --repo <location>
keepsake key verify --repo <location>
keepsake key add-password --repo <location> [--new-password-file <file>] [--label <text>]
keepsake key add-recovery --repo <location> [--recovery-key-out <file>] [--label <text>]
keepsake key remove <id> --repo <location>
Subcommand What it does list Shows all keys: short ID, type, creation time, host and label. * marks the key you unlocked with. verify Checks whether the given password or recovery key opens the repository. It reads only the key files, takes no lock and works while a backup runs. Exit code 4 if the credential is not valid. add-password Adds another password. add-recovery Creates an additional recovery key and shows it once. remove <id> Removes a key, given by its ID or a unique start of it (from key list). The last key cannot be removed. Option Meaning --new-password-file <file> add-password: the new password (first line of the file). Without it you are prompted twice. KEEPSAKE_PASSWORD is not used for the new password. --recovery-key-out <file> add-recovery: also write the new recovery key to this file. --label <text> add-password, add-recovery: label shown in key list. Default: Password or Recovery key.

Warning

Removing a key does not revoke it. Anyone who kept a copy of the old repository key files and knows that password can still open the repository. After a leak, start a new repository and let the old one expire.

keepsake key verify --repo E:\Backups\fileserver --recovery-key-file C:\Keepsake\fileserver-recovery.txt

keepsake key add-password --repo E:\Backups\fileserver --label "Second admin"

keepsake key list --repo E:\Backups\fileserver

docs.title: unlock
docs.text:
Removes stale repository locks, for example after a crash or power loss. By default only locks older than 30 minutes are removed.

keepsake unlock --repo <location> [--all]
Option Meaning --all Also remove current locks. Use it only when no other Keepsake process (service, GUI, another command prompt, another computer) works on the repository. 
keepsake unlock --repo E:\Backups\fileserver

docs.title: sftp-test
docs.text:
Tests which SSH algorithms work between this computer and an SFTP server. It connects once per key exchange, cipher, MAC and host key algorithm and reports which ones work. Nothing is read or written on the server. Use it when a connection fails with "MAC error" on one computer but works on others. The output starts with the .NET Framework release, the Windows version and the FIPS policy. A detailed log is always written: to the --debug-log file, or to %TEMP%\keepsake-debug.log. Send both to support.

keepsake sftp-test --repo sftp://user@host[:port]/path [--sftp-password-file <file> | --sftp-key-file <file>] [--sftp-host-key SHA256:...]

Uses the SFTP options from Common options above. Without --sftp-host-key the host key is shown and you are asked to trust it for the test. With --non-interactive the test then fails. The exit code is 0 once the test has run, whatever the results are.

keepsake sftp-test --repo sftp://backup@nas.example.org/backups/fileserver --sftp-password-file C:\Keepsake\sftp.txt

docs.title: doctor
docs.text:
Checks this computer for everything Keepsake needs and prints one line per check (OK, warning, failure or info): Windows version and Service Pack, .NET Framework 4.8, elevation, the Keepsake service and whether its interface answers, TLS 1.2 and .NET strong crypto (relevant on Windows Server 2008 R2), Volume Shadow Copy, the Event Log source, protection of the data folder, the backup privilege and free space on the system drive. It needs no password.

keepsake doctor [--json]

Exit code 2 if any check failed, 1 if there are warnings, 0 otherwise. Run it elevated, or some checks report only what a normal user can see. See also Windows Server 2008 R2 and Troubleshooting.

keepsake doctor

docs.title: version
docs.text:
Shows the program version and the repository format version.

keepsake version

With --json: {"version": "...", "repositoryFormat": 1}.

docs.title: help
docs.text:
Shows the overview of all commands, or the help of one command.

keepsake help backup

docs.title: Unattended scripts
docs.text:
For scripts and scheduled tasks:

  • Never let a command prompt. Pass --non-interactive, so a missing password fails at once with exit code 3 instead of hanging. Keepsake also switches to non-interactive mode by itself when input is redirected.
  • Pass secrets as files (--password-file, --recovery-key-file, --app-password-file, --sftp-password-file) or through environment variables (KEEPSAKE_PASSWORD, KEEPSAKE_RECOVERY_KEY, KEEPSAKE_APP_PASSWORD, KEEPSAKE_SFTP_PASSWORD, KEEPSAKE_SFTP_KEY_PASSPHRASE). Restrict the files to the account that runs the task. KEEPSAKE_REPOSITORY saves repeating --repo.
  • Use --json for output a script parses. Results go to stdout as JSON, progress is switched off, and errors are printed as {"status": "error", "exitCode": n, "error": "..."}. Exception: jobs export without --out always prints the job JSON.
  • Evaluate the exit code (see Exit codes above), not the text output.
  • Prefer service jobs over scripted backup commands. A job uses VSS, retries, notifications and the run history, and keepsake run <job> --wait returns the result of that run as its exit code.

docs.title: Example: start a job from a scheduled task
docs.text:
A batch file that a scheduled task runs elevated (for example as SYSTEM or an administrator, "Run with highest privileges"):

keepsake run fileserver --wait --non-interactive --app-password-file C:\Keepsake\app-password.txt

The task's last result is then 0 (success), 1 (warnings), 2 (failed) or 6 (cancelled), and the run shows up in History and logs like any other run.

docs.title: Example: monitoring check
docs.text:
A monitoring agent can read the job states as JSON. The jobs array contains each job's name, enabled, lastRun (with state, start and more) and nextRun:

keepsake status --json --non-interactive --app-password-file C:\Keepsake\app-password.txt

For a check that is independent of the service, verify the repository directly, read-only, with a 5 % data sample:

keepsake check --repo \\nas\backup\fileserver --password-file C:\Keepsake\repo-password.txt --read-data-percent 5 --json --non-interactive

Exit code 0 means healthy, 1 warnings, 2 problems found, 4 wrong password, 5 locked (for example a backup is running right now). Also see Monitoring and notifications for e-mail alerts and Event Log IDs.

docs.title: SFTP repositories without a prompt
docs.text:
On the first connection to an SFTP server Keepsake shows the server's host key fingerprint and asks whether to trust it. Unattended runs cannot answer that question and fail instead. Compare the fingerprint once with the one your provider shows or with ssh-keygen -lf <host key file> on the server, then pin it with --sftp-host-key or KEEPSAKE_SFTP_HOST_KEY:

keepsake snapshots --repo sftp://backup@nas.example.org/backups/fileserver --sftp-password-file C:\Keepsake\sftp.txt --sftp-host-key SHA256:nThbg6kXUpJWGl7E1IGOCspRomTxdCARLviKw6E5SY8 --password-file C:\Keepsake\repo-password.txt --non-interactive

If the server presents a different key than the pinned one, the connection is refused (exit code 2). If that happens unexpectedly, find out why before you pin the new key.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page takes you from installation to the first finished backup, and shows how to check that you can get your files back. Plan about ten minutes, plus the time the first backup takes.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need:

  • an administrator account on the computer you back up,
  • a place for the backups that is not the disk you back up: a second disk, a network share, a USB disk or an SFTP server (for example a Hetzner Storage Box),
  • a password manager such as KeePass for the passwords and the recovery key.

On Windows Server 2008 R2, install the prerequisites first: Windows Server 2008 R2.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text: Run Keepsake-<version>.msi as administrator and follow the setup. It installs the programs, starts the Keepsake Backup Service and adds Keepsake Backup and Keepsake Recovery to the Start menu. Details: Installation and upgrade.

docs.title: 2. Set the application password
docs.text:
Start Keepsake Backup from the Start menu and confirm the administrator prompt. On the first start it asks for an Application password (at least 8 characters). It protects access to Keepsake on this computer – the program and the command line. It does not encrypt your backups; that is the repository password of each job.

Replacing a lost computer?

Then you do not need to set anything up: Restore from a backup location… on the same screen opens recovery mode.

docs.title: 3. Create the first job
docs.text:
On the Backup jobs page, click Create the first job (later: + New job). The job editor opens. Enter a Job name at the top, then go through the tabs:

  1. What to back up – tick the folders to back up. Untick a subfolder inside a ticked folder to leave it out. See What to back up and exclusions.
  2. Exclusions – patterns such as *.tmp for files you never need. Also exclude the standard system items (recycle bin, System Volume Information, pagefile and similar) is on by default.
  3. Destination – choose where the backups go, enter a Repository password twice and click Check destination. See Destination.
  4. Schedule – a new job runs daily at 22:00. Change the time or add entries, for example a weekly full backup. See Schedule.
  5. Retention & checks and Options – the defaults are a good start: see Retention and checks and Options.

Click Save. Keepsake creates the encrypted repository and shows its recovery key once.

docs.title: 4. Store the recovery key
docs.text:
The recovery key (KS1-…) opens your backups when the password is lost – on any computer. Click Copy KeePass entry and paste it into a new KeePass entry: it contains the location, the host key, the recovery key and how to restore. Add the repository password (and the SFTP or share password, if any) to the same entry. Then tick I have stored the recovery key in a safe place outside this server and click Done.

Keep a copy of the KeePass database off this computer. Which password or key you need when: Passwords and keys.

docs.title: 5. Run the first backup
docs.text: Click Run now on the job. The card shows the progress; the first backup reads and stores everything, later runs only store what changed. When it has finished, the card shows Last backup OK – or a warning if some files could not be read; History shows which ones and why. See History and logs.

docs.title: 6. Check that you can get your files back
docs.text:
A backup you have never restored from is a hope, not a backup:

  1. On the job, click Check keys and test the password and the recovery key from KeePass.
  2. On the Restore page, restore a folder into a new folder and open some files. See Restoring files.
  3. Once, before you rely on Keepsake: do the recovery test at the end of the disaster recovery runbook on a second computer, using only the KeePass entry.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Get an e-mail when a backup fails: enter the SMTP server under Settings and switch on the notifications on the job's Retention & checks tab.
  • Feed the Windows Event Log into your monitoring: Monitoring and notifications.
  • Back up to a second place as well (another job with another destination), for example USB disks you take off site.

docs.title: History and logs
docs.text: The History & logs page lists every run of the Keepsake service: backups, restores, integrity checks and cleanups, with their result. Double-click a run to open its detail window with the summary, the list of everything that was not backed up and why, the phase timings and the full log. The service keeps run logs for a configurable time and stores them as files under %ProgramData%\Keepsake.

docs.title: The run list
docs.text:
The list shows the newest 200 runs, newest first, and refreshes by itself while the page is open. Use the drop-down at the top right to show All jobs or a single job.

Column Content Result State of the run (see below), with a coloured dot. Started Local start time. Job Job name. Type Backup, Full backup, Restore, Check or Cleanup. Trigger Manual, Schedule, Missed (catch-up after the service was not running) or Retry <n>. Duration Run time; … while the run is queued or running. Files Backups: number of files, plus (<n> not backed up) if any were skipped. Restores: <n> restored. Data Backups: <new> new / <stored> stored. Restores: bytes written. Message Short reason for a failure or warning.

To open a run, double-click it, or select it and click Show details.

Note

Restores in recovery mode do not run in the service and do not appear here.

docs.title: Run types
docs.text: Type What it does Backup / Full backup Backs up the job's sources. A full backup reads every file again. Restore Restores files from a backup (see Restoring files). Check Verifies the repository structure and decrypts a share of the data (see Retention and checks). Cleanup Applies the retention rules and frees the space of removed backups.

docs.title: Run states
docs.text:
State Meaning Queued Waiting to start, for example because the maximum number of parallel jobs is reached. Running In progress. Success Finished without problems. Warning Finished, but with problems: some items were not backed up or not restored. A backup with warnings still created a usable backup of everything else. Failed The run did not complete. A failed backup creates no backup. Cancelled Stopped by a user, or still queued when the service stopped unexpectedly.

Items that are excluded by a pattern are listed as skipped but do not cause a warning. Locked or unreadable files, missing source folders, files deleted or changed during the backup, links that are not followed and VSS problems do.

If the service stops unexpectedly (crash, power loss), runs that were still running are marked Failed with Interrupted: the service stopped unexpectedly. at the next start; queued runs are marked Cancelled.

docs.title: The run detail window
docs.text:
The window title shows job and start time. At the top you see the state with the message, then the summary:

  • run ID, type and trigger
  • start, end and duration
  • backups: new, changed, unchanged and not backed-up files, number of folders; total size, bytes read, new data and stored size after compression
  • restores: restored, already up to date, kept and failed files, bytes written
  • the short ID of the backup (snapshot) that was written or restored

docs.title: Not backed up / problems
docs.text:
This tab lists every item that was not processed or needs attention, with Kind, Path and Reason.

Kind Meaning Error The item was not backed up or restored (for example Access denied., Path is too long.). Counted as "not processed". Warning Processed with a problem (for example File changed while it was being backed up; the stored copy may be inconsistent.). Skipped Left out on purpose (excluded by a pattern, or an existing file kept during a restore).
  • The filter drop-down shows Problems (errors and warnings, default), Errors, Warnings, Skipped or All.
  • The search box filters by path or reason.
  • The counter next to it shows <n> not processed · <n> warnings · <n> skipped.
  • The list shows at most 5,000 entries. Export all as CSV… saves the complete list (all kinds, unfiltered) as a semicolon-separated UTF-8 file with the columns Kind;Path;Message;Time.

Troubleshooting explains the common reasons.

docs.title: Phases
docs.text: Each phase of the run with its start time (UTC) and duration in seconds. Use it to see where a slow run spends its time.

docs.title: Full log
docs.text: The complete readable log of the run, as it is stored on disk. Copy it from here for support.

docs.title: Log retention
docs.text: The service deletes old run logs once a day. A run is removed when it is older than Keep run logs for (days) or when the job has more than … and at most (runs per job) newer runs. The defaults are 90 days and 200 runs per job. Change them in Settings.

docs.title: Where the logs live on disk
docs.text:
All files are below the service's data folder, by default %ProgramData%\Keepsake (the Settings page shows the actual Data folder). Only SYSTEM and Administrators can read it.

File Content runs\<job ID>\<run ID>.record.json Run record: state, times, counts, message. runs\<job ID>\<run ID>.detail.json Phases and issue list. runs\<job ID>\<run ID>.log Readable full log. logs\service.log Diagnostic log of the service itself (start, stop, schedules, settings changes, errors). Rotated at 10 MB, 5 files kept (service.log.1 … .5). logs\debug.log Optional SFTP debug log, only when switched on in Settings.

The command line shows the same information: keepsake runs [<job>] lists runs and keepsake log <run-id> prints a run's full log. See Command line.

docs.title: Installation and upgrade
docs.text: Keepsake comes as an MSI installer for the computers you back up, and as a portable ZIP for restoring on any computer without installing anything. This page covers both, upgrades and uninstalling.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Windows Server 2008 R2 SP1 or Windows 10/11, 64-bit.
  • .NET Framework 4.8 (included in current Windows 10/11; on 2008 R2 install it first).
  • Administrator rights: the program, the service and most commands run elevated.

Windows Server 2008 R2 needs a few more prerequisites (Service Pack 1, .NET 4.8, TLS 1.2 for e-mail): Windows Server 2008 R2.

docs.title: Download and check
docs.text:
Download Keepsake-<version>.msi or Keepsake-<version>-portable.zip from the release and compare its SHA-256 with SHA256SUMS.txt of the same release:

powershell -Command "Get-FileHash .\Keepsake-0.9.14.msi -Algorithm SHA256"

Unsigned releases

As long as the releases are not code-signed, Windows SmartScreen may warn when you start the MSI. Check the checksum, then choose More info → Run anyway. Signed releases show Kraus-Ahma IT Consulting as publisher.

docs.title: Install with the MSI
docs.text:
Run the MSI as administrator. The setup lets you choose the install folder (default C:\Program Files\dkait\keepsake). It:

  • installs the programs: KeepsakeGui.exe (the Keepsake Backup program), keepsake.exe (command line) and keepsake-service.exe (the service),
  • registers and starts the Keepsake Backup Service (LocalSystem, starts automatically, restarts after a failure),
  • adds the install folder to the PATH, so keepsake works in every new command prompt,
  • adds Keepsake Backup and Keepsake Recovery to the Start menu,
  • creates the data folder %ProgramData%\Keepsake and restricts it (and the install folder) to SYSTEM and Administrators.

The MSI refuses to install without .NET Framework 4.8, on 32-bit Windows, or on 2008 R2 without Service Pack 1.

Then start Keepsake Backup and continue with Getting started.

docs.title: Check the installation
docs.text:
In an elevated command prompt:

keepsake doctor

doctor checks Windows version, .NET, the service, the data folder permissions, VSS, the Event Log source, TLS 1.2, the backup privilege and free space. Everything should be OK or INFO.

docs.title: Where Keepsake keeps its data
docs.text: Location Contents Install folder Programs, this help (help\), Enable-Tls12.ps1, Keepsake Recovery.cmd %ProgramData%\Keepsake\config\ Jobs and settings; passwords encrypted with Windows DPAPI for the service %ProgramData%\Keepsake\runs\ Record, issue list and log of every run %ProgramData%\Keepsake\logs\ Service log, optional debug log The repositories Wherever the jobs write them – Keepsake never stores backups in its own folders

docs.title: Upgrade
docs.text:
Run the MSI of the new version. It replaces the programs and keeps the jobs, settings, run history and the application password. The setup stops the service and starts it again: start the upgrade when no backup is running. A backup interrupted by the upgrade is not lost – the next run reuses what was already stored.

An older MSI cannot be installed over a newer version ("A newer version of Keepsake is already installed").

Newer versions always read repositories written by older ones.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
Uninstall Keepsake Backup under Settings → Apps (or Programs and Features). This removes the programs, the service and the Start menu entries. It keeps:

  • %ProgramData%\Keepsake – jobs, settings and history; a later installation picks them up again,
  • all repositories – your backups are never touched.

To remove everything, delete %ProgramData%\Keepsake after uninstalling.

docs.title: Portable version
docs.text:
The portable ZIP contains the same programs without the installer. Unpack it to a local folder (not to the backup storage) on any Windows computer with .NET Framework 4.8. Use it to:

  • restore without installing anything: double-click Keepsake Recovery.cmd – see Recovery mode,
  • work with a repository on the command line (keepsake snapshots, keepsake restore, …) – see Command line.

The portable version does not install the service, so it does not run scheduled backups.

Keep the portable ZIP of the version you use, with its checksum, in the KeePass entry of your backups. Every repository also contains a copy of keepsake.exe in tools\, but that copy is not encrypted and could have been replaced by whoever controls the storage – see the disaster recovery runbook for how to check it.

docs.title: Destination
docs.text:
The Destination tab decides where a job stores its backups and with which password they are encrypted. The backups go into an encrypted repository in a folder, on a network share, on one or more USB disks or on an SFTP server. Keepsake creates the repository when you save the job, or uses an existing one.

Under Where are the backups stored? choose Folder or network share, USB disk or SFTP server.

docs.title: Folder or network share
docs.text:
Enter the path in Folder (local disk or \server\share\folder) or pick it with Browse…. The path must be absolute, for example E:\Backups\Fileserver or \\nas\backup\fileserver.

For a network path, Keepsake connects with the computer account (the service runs as LocalSystem) unless you enter an account of its own:

Field Content User (DOMAIN\user) Account for the share, DOMAIN\user or server\user. Password Its password. If a password is already stored, the field stays empty; leave it empty to keep the stored one.

The credentials are used only for the connection to this share.

docs.title: USB disk
docs.text:
Keepsake recognises USB disks by their volume ID, not by drive letter, so the disk is found whatever letter Windows gives it.

  1. Connect the disk.
  2. Select it in the list and click Add disk. Click Refresh if a disk you just connected is missing.
  3. Enter Folder on the disk (without drive letter), for example Keepsake\Fileserver. The default is Keepsake.

Disks of this job lists the registered disks with label, size and connected as E: or not connected. Remove unregisters a disk; the data on it stays.

docs.title: Several disks (rotation)
docs.text:
Register several disks to rotate them, for example one on site and one off site. Each disk holds its own, independent repository with the same repository password. A backup goes to the first registered disk that is connected. If none is connected, the run fails with None of the USB disks of this job is connected.

When you save, Keepsake creates the repository on the connected disk. For every other disk, connect it, click Refresh and then Prepare this disk next to it. This creates the repository on that disk and shows its own recovery key. If no disk is connected when you save, the job is saved anyway; prepare each disk later.

Warning

Every disk gets a different recovery key. Store each one in KeePass.

docs.title: SFTP server
docs.text: Field Content Server Host name or IP address. Port Default 22. User SFTP user name. Password / Private key How Keepsake logs in. SFTP password For password login. Leave empty to keep a stored password. Load key file… For key login: an OpenSSH or PuTTY (.ppk) private key file. The key is stored on this server; load a new file to replace it. Key passphrase (if the key is protected) Passphrase of the private key. Remote folder Absolute path on the server, for example /backups/fileserver.

docs.title: Host key
docs.text:
On the first connection, Keepsake shows the server's host key (SHA256:...) and asks whether to trust it. Compare it with the fingerprint on the server (ssh-keygen -lf on the server's key file) before you confirm. The trusted key is then shown as Trusted host key: .... Forget removes it; the next check asks again.

If the server later presents a different key, Keepsake warns that the host key has CHANGED and shows the new and the trusted key. This can mean the server was reinstalled, or that the connection is intercepted. Only trust the new key if the server administrator confirms it. Scheduled runs do not connect to a server whose key changed.

docs.title: Hetzner Storage Box
docs.text: For a host ending in .your-storagebox.de, a new job starts on port 23. Port 23 is OpenSSH and offers authenticated encryption (AES-GCM); port 22 is ProFTPD and only offers AES-CTR.
